summary.text: Representability is unchanged when the two quadratic coefficients are swapped, since one may simultaneously exchange the corresponding variables. However, the proposed list contains \((1,2,1,1)\) but omits its swap \((2,1,1,1)\), so it cannot characterize exactly the universally representing forms.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
R(a,b,c,d)
\]
denote the assertion that \(a,b,c,d\) are positive integers and that every nonnegative integer \(n\) has a representation
\[
n=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4
\]
with \(x,y,z,w\ge 0\) integers. Let \(S\) be the set of the 49 quadruples displayed in the conjecture. The conjecture asserts that, for every quadruple of nonnegative integers \((a,b,c,d)\),
\[
R(a,b,c,d)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (a,b,c,d)\in S.
\]
(The positivity requirement in \(R\) makes this equivalent to the stated formulation for positive coefficients.)

The key observation is that representability is unchanged when the first two coefficients are interchanged. More precisely,
\[
R(a,b,c,d)\Longrightarrow R(b,a,c,d).
\]
Indeed, suppose \(R(a,b,c,d)\) holds. The coefficients \(b,a,c,d\) are still positive. Given any nonnegative integer \(n\), choose nonnegative integers \(x,y,z,w\) such that
\[
n=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4.
\]
Set
\[
X=y,\qquad Y=x,\qquad Z=z,\qquad W=w.
\]
Then, using commutativity of addition,
\[
\begin{aligned}
bX^2+aY^2+cZ^3+dW^4
&=by^2+ax^2+cz^3+dw^4\\
&=ax^2+by^2+cz^3+dw^4\\
&=n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus every \(n\) represented by the form with coefficients \((a,b,c,d)\) is also represented by the form with coefficients \((b,a,c,d)\). Interchanging the variables once more gives the converse as well, so in fact
\[
R(a,b,c,d)\Longleftrightarrow R(b,a,c,d).
\]
Only the forward implication will be needed.

Now assume, for contradiction, that the conjectured classification is correct for all coefficients. The quadruple
\[
(1,2,1,1)
\]
is explicitly the first member of the proposed set \(S\). Therefore, by the “membership implies full representability” direction of the conjectured equivalence,
\[
R(1,2,1,1)
\]
holds. Concretely, the conjecture thereby asserts that every nonnegative integer \(n\) can be written as
\[
n=x^2+2y^2+z^3+w^4
\]
for some nonnegative integers \(x,y,z,w\).

Apply the symmetry just proved, interchanging the two square variables. For any such representation, put \(X=y\) and \(Y=x\). Then
\[
n=x^2+2y^2+z^3+w^4
  =2X^2+Y^2+z^3+w^4.
\]
Hence every nonnegative integer is represented by the form with coefficient quadruple
\[
(2,1,1,1),
\]
and all four of these coefficients are positive. Thus
\[
R(2,1,1,1)
\]
holds.

The other direction of the conjectured equivalence, now applied to \((2,1,1,1)\), would force
\[
(2,1,1,1)\in S.
\]
But this quadruple is absent from the displayed list. To make the finite check explicit, the listed quadruples whose first coordinate is \(2\) are
\[
(2,3,1,1),\ (2,4,1,1),\ (2,4,1,2),\ (2,3,1,4),\ (2,3,1,5),\ (2,4,1,5),\ (2,4,1,11).
\]
None has second coordinate \(1\), so none is \((2,1,1,1)\). Therefore
\[
(2,1,1,1)\notin S,
\]
contradicting the consequence obtained from the conjecture.

Consequently the proposed biconditional classification cannot be true. Its failure is forced by the fact that the representability property is symmetric under swapping the two quadratic coefficients, whereas the proposed list contains \((1,2,1,1)\) but omits the symmetric quadruple \((2,1,1,1)\). This disproves the conjecture.
